system:
You audit the knowledge atoms of one Knowledge Card. A card is the answer key for a benchmark of expert conceptual knowledge, so every atom must be correct, self-contained, and assessable on its own.

Judge every atom on every check listed below. Rules:
- For checks about evidence, use only the evidence sentences supplied with the atom. Do not repair an atom with your own knowledge.
- For GROUNDED, use "hold" when unreadable PDF symbols prevent verification; explain what is needed. Use fail only when the available evidence is sufficient to determine that the claim is unsupported. This hold rule takes precedence over the strictness rule. Judge other checks independently using their listed values; do not invent missing facts.
- Be strict within each check's allowed values. Do not turn an inability to verify GROUNDED into revise or fail; use hold as defined above.
- "why" is required for every value other than the first listed value; keep it under 30 words. Omit "why" when passing.

Checks (allowed values in brackets; the first value means no problem):
- GROUNDED [pass / revise / fail / hold]: The cited evidence sentences state the atom, including its specificity, causal force, assumptions, and certainty. pass = fully stated. revise = partly stated (the atom adds, drops, or strengthens something; say what). fail = not stated when the available evidence permits a judgment. hold = unreadable symbols prevent verification. For pass or revise, put the supporting evidence ids in cite.
- SINGLE_CLAIM [pass / revise]: The atom is one independently assessable claim. revise = it joins two or more claims that could be true or false separately. Evidence spanning more than three sentences is not by itself a reason to split or revise an atom.
- SCOPE_LABEL [pass / revise]: The S label fits (S1 what it is / S2 how it works / S3 where it ends). revise = wrong label; put the right one in why, e.g. 'S2: ...'.
- L1_ONLY [pass / fail]: The atom is recall-level knowledge. fail = knowing it requires applying the concept to a new problem, or combining facts from distant passages.
- SOURCE_INDEPENDENT [pass / revise / fail]: A domain expert who never read this book could judge the claim true or false. revise = phrased as the authors' statement but the claim itself is general (drop the attribution). fail = an isolated study finding, conjecture, or author-specific opinion, classification, or recommendation, even if attribution was removed. Explicitly scoped established facts about a formalism or architecture and conditional theoretical results remain eligible.
- NO_OVERLAP [pass / fail]: No other atom in this card states or contains the same claim. If two atoms overlap, fail only the less informative one and put the other atom's id in cite; the other one passes.
- CENTRALITY [pass / fail]: The atom matters for understanding the concept. fail = peripheral detail.
Whole-card checks (report under "batch"):
- CONCEPT_SCOPE [pass / fail]: The concept is a general concept of the field. fail = a topic whose assessable content is restricted to excluded study-specific findings or author-specific positions. A named formalism, system, or architecture is not disqualified solely for being specific if its scoped conceptual facts are source-independent.

Output ONLY one JSON object:
{"units": {"<atom_id>": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": "", "cite": []}, ...}, ...}, "batch": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": ""}}}
user:
CONCEPT: Mean systemic filling pressure
ASSESSMENT SCOPE: Mean systemic (circulatory filling) pressure as the upstream pressure for venous return in the Guytonian model: its relation to stressed and unstressed volume and venous capacitance, the venous return gradient with right atrial pressure and resistance to venous return, and how volume loading or vasoactive agents change it. Excludes clinical bolus decisions and case vignettes.

ATOMS:
- MED-PHYS-C03-S1-01 | S1
  ATOM: Mean systemic filling pressure (MSFP) represents the pressure generated by elastic recoil of the systemic circulation during a no-flow state.
  EVIDENCE:
    [MED-PHYS-p0151-s04] Mean systemic filling pressure (MSFP) represents the pressure generated by elastic recoil of the systemic circulation during a no-flow state.
- MED-PHYS-C03-S1-02 | S1
  ATOM: Mean systemic pressure (Pms) is defined as the equilibrium pressure only in the systemic circulation in the absence of any flow, ignoring the heart and pulmonary circulation (e.g. by clamping the aorta and venae cavae).
  EVIDENCE:
    [MED-PHYS-p0132-s12] [3] A closely related and more widely used term is mean systemic pressure (Pms) defined as the equilibrium pressure only in the systemic circulation in the absence of any flow, ignoring the heart and pulmonary circulation (e.g. by clamping the aorta and venae cavae).
- MED-PHYS-C03-S1-03 | S1
  ATOM: In the Guytonian model of venous return, mean systemic pressure (Pms) is the upstream pressure and right atrial pressure (RAP) is the downstream pressure, so the difference between Pms and RAP is the net driving pressure for venous return to the heart.
  EVIDENCE:
    [MED-PHYS-p0132-s14] Years later, Guyton proposed Pms as the upstream pressure for the venous return [4].
    [MED-PHYS-p0132-s15] He described the right atrial pressure (RAP) as the downstream pressure with the difference between Pms and RAP as the net driving pressure for venous return to the heart.
- MED-PHYS-C03-S2-01 | S2
  ATOM: Venous return is directly proportional to the pressure gradient between mean systemic filling pressure (MSFP) and right atrial pressure (RAP) and inversely proportional to the resistance of the vessels ($R_v$), i.e. $VR \propto (\mathrm{MSFP} - \mathrm{RAP})/R_v$.
  EVIDENCE:
    [MED-PHYS-p0151-s08] Venous return is directly proportional to the pressure gradient between MSFP and RAP
    [MED-PHYS-p0151-s09] and inversely proportional to the resistance of the vessels (Rv).
- MED-PHYS-C03-S2-02 | S2
  ATOM: Stressed volume, and with it mean systemic pressure (Pms), can be increased in only two ways: by increasing circulatory volume (for example by fluid loading) or by decreasing venous capacitance (for example by increasing sympathetic tone with norepinephrine or other vasopressors).
  EVIDENCE:
    [MED-PHYS-p0133-s06] There can be only two ways to increase “stressed volume” (and Pms in this process), either by increasing circulatory volume (e.g. by fluid loading) or by decreasing venous capacitance (e.g. by increasing sympathetic tone with norepinephrine or other vasopressors).
- MED-PHYS-C03-S2-03 | S2
  ATOM: Mean systemic pressure (Pms) results from elastic recoil potential stored in the walls of the components of the circulatory system and is determined by the stressed volume, the volume of blood that stretches the vessels beyond their normal shape.
  EVIDENCE:
    [MED-PHYS-p0133-s02] Pms is the result of elastic recoil potential, stored in the walls of the components of the circulatory system and is determined by the volume of blood that stretches the vessels further beyond their normal shape (so-called stressed volume).
- MED-PHYS-C03-S3-01 | S3
  ATOM: Mean circulatory filling pressure (Pmcf) is the average pressure in the whole circulation when the heart is stopped momentarily and the pressure in the entire circulatory system equilibrates, whereas mean systemic pressure (Pms) is the equilibrium pressure only in the systemic circulation in the absence of any flow, ignoring the heart and pulmonary circulation.
  EVIDENCE:
    [MED-PHYS-p0132-s11] They coined the term mean circulatory filling pressure (Pmcf), described as the average pressure in the circulation when the heart is stopped momentarily and the pressure in the entire circulatory system equilibrates, for example after administration of the cardioplegic solution.
    [MED-PHYS-p0132-s12] [3] A closely related and more widely used term is mean systemic pressure (Pms) defined as the equilibrium pressure only in the systemic circulation in the absence of any flow, ignoring the heart and pulmonary circulation (e.g. by clamping the aorta and venae cavae).
- MED-PHYS-C03-S3-02.r1 | S2
  ATOM: Under normal circumstances, when blood volume remains near constant, the major factor determining the return of blood to the heart is resistance to venous return, which arises from changes in the resistance of blood vessels at the level of organs.
  EVIDENCE:
    [MED-PHYS-p0133-s07] Under normal circumstances, the blood volume remains near constant.
    [MED-PHYS-p0133-s08] Thus, the major
    [MED-PHYS-p0133-s09] factor that determines the return of blood to the heart is resistance to venous return, produced as a result of changes in resistance of blood vessels at the level of organs [2].
- MED-PHYS-C03-S3-03.r1 | S2
  ATOM: During active flow, mean systemic filling pressure (Pms, or mean circulatory filling pressure, Pmcf) is determined primarily by the pressure in the venous side of the circulation, because the larger volume of blood is stored in the high-capacitance venous system.
  EVIDENCE:
    [MED-PHYS-p0132-s13] Bayliss and Starling also realized that during active flow, Pms (or Pmcf) is determined primarily by the pressure in the venous side of the circulation as the larger volume of blood is stored in the high-capacitance venous system.
